title: Personal Financial Management Practices Among Selected Personnel of the Bureau of the Treasury – Central Office
venue: Guild of Educators in TESOL International Journal, Volume I Issue 2
tldr: A descriptive survey of 183 Bureau of Treasury personnel finds agreement on financial planning, money management, income protection, and investment practices, with highest scores for goal-setting and saving to avoid borrowing.
problem_and_motivation: Personal financial management practices among government employees directly affect organizational productivity and national wealth. No existing study had examined the financial practices of personnel at the Bureau of the Treasury – Central Office, despite its central role in managing national finances.
approach: Descriptive survey design using a researcher-constructed questionnaire administered to 183 personnel across 35 divisions, selected via simple random probability sampling.
Instrument achieved Cronbach’s Alpha of 0.896 in pre-testing, indicating high internal consistency and reliability.

Survey covered four PFM dimensions: Financial Planning (5 items), Money Management (10 items), Income and Asset Protection (5 items), and Investments (5 items), each with 5-point Likert scale responses.
Data analysis used descriptive statistics (percentage, frequency, weighted mean, ranking) and inferential statistics (T-test and one-way ANOVA) to test differences across demographic groups.

Respondents were predominantly female (60.1%), single (63.9%), aged 26–35 (37.7%), bachelor’s degree holders (78.7%), rank-and-file (78.1%), permanent (86.9%), with 5 years or fewer tenure (53.0%) and monthly compensation of P15,001–P30,000 (38.8%).
findings: num: Financial planning obtained the highest overall weighted mean of 4.26 (Agree), with goal-setting ranking first at 4.39.
num: Money management overall weighted mean was 4.02 (Agree); saving to avoid borrowing ranked highest at 4.47, while credit card use ranked lowest at 2.99.
num: Income and asset protection overall weighted mean was 3.58 (Agree); considering future uncertainties ranked highest at 4.30, while non-life insurance acquisition ranked lowest at 2.96.
num: Investments overall weighted mean was 3.15 (Moderately Agree); purchasing government securities ranked highest at 3.79.

The study found no significant differences in PFM assessments when respondents were grouped by age, sex, civil status, educational attainment, job position, employment status, tenure, or monthly compensation.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides empirical baseline data on personal financial management practices among Philippine government employees, specifically at the Bureau of the Treasury. It operationalizes PFM across four standardized dimensions (financial planning, money management, income and asset protection, investments) and measures each with Likert-scale instruments. The finding that debt-averse saving behavior dominates among rank-and-file government workers contributes descriptive evidence to the literature on Filipino financial behavior. The study also demonstrates that demographic variables do not significantly differentiate PFM practices within this population, suggesting uniform financial engagement across employee profiles.
directly_justifies: Government employees prioritize saving to avoid borrowing over credit-based purchasing (money management rank 1).
Financial goal-setting is the highest-rated financial planning practice among Bureau of Treasury personnel.
Non-life insurance and derivatives market participation are the lowest-rated PFM practices, indicating gaps in financial product awareness.
Demographic variables (age, sex, education, tenure) do not significantly differentiate PFM assessment scores.
limits: Single-agency scope (Bureau of Treasury only) limits generalizability to other government or private-sector populations.
Self-reported Likert-scale data may reflect perceived rather than actual financial practices.
Study does not examine digital or app-based financial management tools, limiting relevance to PFMS design.
No longitudinal dimension; captures only a single snapshot of practices.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan of all 14 topic domains was conducted. Domains flagged as relevant: Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals) — codes 1.B (medium, salary data) and 1.C (high, core financial behavior assessment); Domain 2 (Culturally Specific Practices) — code 2.A (medium, documents debt-averse culture and social media influence); Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) — code 3.A (low, uses four broad PFM categories but no granular classification); Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) — code 5.A (medium, profiles respondents by weighted mean scores); Domain 7 (Budgeting Strategies) — code 7.A (high, directly measures budget plan adherence); Domain 13 (Savings and Debt) — codes 13.A (high, saving behavior) and 13.B (high, credit/debt aversion). Rejected domains: Domain 4 (Personal Finance Systems) — no system evaluation or landscape discussion; Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) — no algorithmic or forecasting content; Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection), Domain 9 (Mobile-First), Domain 10 (Privacy/Security), Domain 11 (Engagement), Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks), Domain 14 (ML/Deployment) — entirely absent from the paper. The paper provides moderate topical coverage relevant to understanding Filipino financial behavior but does not address system design or algorithmic approaches.

limitations: Single-agency scope limits generalizability across Philippine government or private-sector populations. [unacknowledged]
Self-reported Likert-scale measures may reflect perceived rather than actual financial management practices. [unacknowledged]
No longitudinal or repeated-measures design; results represent a single cross-sectional snapshot. [unacknowledged]
No examination of digital financial tools, mobile apps, or PFMS technology adoption. [unacknowledged]
Sample drawn during COVID-19 period (data collected 2021) which may have influenced financial behaviors abnormally.
remember_this: Saving to avoid borrowing is the top money management practice (weighted mean 4.47).
Financial goal-setting ranks highest in financial planning (weighted mean 4.39).
Non-life insurance (2.96) and derivatives (2.62) have the lowest adoption rates.
Demographic variables do not significantly differentiate PFM practices in this population.
Government employees show strong debt aversion and preference for saving over credit.
